subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Objective vs. Subjective Truth
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Objective vs. Subjective Truth.

hook.text: 'The Earth is 4.5 billion years old' & 'chocolate is the best flavor' are both called 'true.' They're not the same.

buildup.text: Objective truth: true regardless of what anyone thinks. Subjective truth: true for the individual's experience.

discovery.text: Science deals in objective truths (or approximations). Aesthetics, taste, and personal experience are subjective.

twist.text: The confusion: treating subjective truths as objective or dismissing objective truths as subjective.

climax.text: Both matter. But confusing which category a claim belongs to derails every conversation.

punchline.text: Your experience is real. That doesn't make it universal.

quiz.question: What distinguishes objective truth from subjective truth?
options: Objective truths hold regardless of individual perspective

details.summary: Objective truths hold regardless of anyone's beliefs or feelings, like mathematical facts. Subjective truths depend on individual perspective, like taste preferences. Many disputes arise from confusing these categories.
details.whyItMatters: Treating subjective preferences as objective facts fuels unresolvable arguments, while treating objective facts as mere opinion undermines shared reality.
takeaways: Objective truths are independent of personal perspective
Subjective truths depend on individual experience or preference
The confusion between them drives many pointless disagreements

faq.question: How can you tell whether a claim is objective or subjective?
faq.answer: Ask: would this be true even if no one believed it? Gravity exists regardless of opinion — that's objective. Chocolate tasting good depends on who is eating it — that's subjective. The test is independence from any observer.

faq.question: Are moral claims objective or subjective in nature?
faq.answer: This is one of the deepest philosophical debates. Moral realists argue that some ethical truths are objective. Moral relativists argue they are subjective. The answer you accept shapes your entire approach to ethics and law.
